The essay commencers by dealing with what is called the " bias in favour of war," and paases on to the causes of war, which are described as want 4,f inquiry, iudifferenve to human misery, national irritability, self-interest. the secret motives id cabinets, and ideas of glory. As hearing moon the latter, (lifters's "Decline and Full" is quoted with effect. "An long as mankind," says (linuoN, " shall continue to bestow more liberal applause on their destroyers than 011 their benefaetors, the . thirst if military glory will ever be the vice of the most exelt•si charaeters." Lord SHAFTESBURY rornackcil that it was strange that "war, which of all things appears the most savage should be the 1111SS1,01 of the moat heroic spirits." Carr it he that the explanation as to this is given by ERASMUS who observes thitt 'war doee more harm In, the morals of men than even to their property and per mart." The Duke of Wittusoros may be cited 106 an authority absolittely beyond dispute, anti ire4,flee said :—" War is the most rlutestable Lining. If you had seen but one tie), of war, you would pray God you might never see another." The Clerk stated that the complainant took out a summons against her husband, but subsequently her father applied to tle: magistrates for a war- rant against the defendant, AA 110 said he did not think his daughter MIA safe whilst Le was at liberty. -The complainant stepped into the witness box, hut declined to give evidence against her husband, remarking that she did not wish him to be sent to prison this time. —Alderman Burgess. if yell do give evidence I shall retnand the case till Nlonday. She still hesitated to give evidence and the magistrates asked her to leave the box and celled on the next rase. -When the case was again called on, complainant said her husband struck her! on the fare. Ile alno " ground his teeth at her: - Complainant's father said defendant had often abused his wife, bet the latter denied having made ! !tie of thretes, and said he bad received provocation. Alderman Burgess (to defendant) : You are only IS years of age. It is a pity you cannot start life in auntie manner. Let this he a warning to you. We are dispose.] to give you an opportunity to take your wife home. We let you off this morning, but I if you are brought here again you must understand I • that the punishment will be equal to the offence. Yon will, however, have to pay the costs of the ease. —Mr. arnett : You are indebted to your wife I for the lenient sentence. She does not wish you , to be sent to prison. A BUTCHER PAID TO SHOUT. I John Thompson, who is employed by John Bull and Company. butchers, Lyme-street, was charged at Warrington, on Saturday, with com- mitting a breach of the peace in Lyme-street, and I lorsemarket-st an the 271 h April.—P.C. liolliags- woetti said that on Saturday, the 27th tilt., at live p.m., he was in I lorsemarket-st., when lie SAW the defendant standing outside the hotelier's shop at the corner of Lyme-st. Ile was standing on the , footpath in Ilontemarket-st., and was shooting con- tinually. At sin o'clock he cautioned the defendant, and said hisconduct could not be allowed. Defend- ant walked away from him awl said " I know my little business. I know how fuel can go." Witness drew a sergeant's attention to the conduct of the man, and subsequently Inspector Spinks spoke to him, but the defendant would not listen, and began to shout " We will show them bow to sell beef Don't he loft halfpenny apsand. Five pounds for a shilling. Talk about breaking us ; they can't bend us. When the Ship Canal is made we shall have lota of money." THE SCOTTISH LANOITAML—But again, our poor di. natured young victim of false methods may allege that she would gladly sing Scotch songs if they were only written in English; but the Scotch language is too broad and guttural for her, and so with a wise abstention she early makes lip her mind to let it drop. Poor creature! sweet little sophist ! who has been trained away from the sweetness and roundness of her native Scottish dia- lect, and traincl into the clippings and the mincinge and the sibilations of the unmusical English tongue; who, perhaps, while she eschews a Sentch song for the diffi- culty of saving loch instead of like, will trill ;.-cou off a , German in which the same guttural occurs 5iX times for once that it occurs in the Scotch; and whose ! organs are too refined, she deems, for brwsd Scotch, at the'svery moment when she is learning Italian in order to' improve her voice with the musical broad Italian it, which is attire same time the distinctive and dominant vowel-sound in every popular Scotch tong! Nothing ' can be more silly, indeed, and Inoro significant of the, false culture and gross ignorance so common in what is I called a fashionable society," than the manner in w h hic ! they talk of the beautiful Scotch language, which indeed ! is not, properly speakinz a different language, but only ! tire most uncorrupted and the most mueical dialect of , our common English tongue--" that noble Doric which," ass fine poetical genius did not hesitate to say," is at once rustic and dignified, heroic and vernacular." It is sad indeed, and shameful, that well-dressed young gen- tlemen and ladies with Scottish, blood in their veins ehould affiive themselves to talk contemptuously of a language which one attire most original and most cul- tured of modern English poet-thinkers is proud to tate but this is only novel the unfortunate fro:sits of the process of denationalising our upper classes by wish- ing them pendants to a centralising metropolis outside of their natural home, and of the lamentable omission of the national element in our schools aad colleges noted above, which leaves to the chance fancy of an occasional amateur what ought to have been the sacred care of a united people—./.a Efackio -

Minter CCURoo.—There is among the North American Indians a very beautiful liitend about a mystical bird that steals through the pine groves at ginaming time in Saintlier, whets the moron is at the full, and enchants the wigwams with the thrill of sweet songs from tile spirit world, and the lost and loved Oiler who are far away in the " happy hunting-grounds:. This mystical bird has been happily compared by Hugh Macmillan to the English cuckoo, which conies to us when the year is at its high tide of bloom anti beauty, and vanishes with the wanitA of spring. There ha a pleasant verse among thin Gloucestershire peasantry which tells an that— • •- ••
..il;ruckno comas In April, Sings a song In May, Then in June another lane And then he Mee away. . . •
The cuckoo is universally regarded Os Via country as the usweet harbinger of spring." IS is the male bird which ' '' • ' "

gives the well-known' sound. the voice of the female cuckoo being a harsh screaming chatter. In the mid- land counties it is regiirded as somethins uncommon for the cuckoo-cry to be heard before April 20th, which is the annual fair-day at Tenbury in Worcestershire; and it is regarded as equally strange if the cuckoo is heard after June 26th, which is the fair-day of Pershore in the Sams county. There is a superstition among the uneducated classes in Norfolk that what you are doing when you first hear the cry of the cuckoo you will be doing very frequently throughout the year. In Norfolk there was a belief among the peasantry that if a young woman on first hearing the cuckoo took off her shoe, she would find in it a hair of the aame colour on that on the head oilier future husband. Cornishmen regard it as of good omen if they hear the first cry of .cuckoo" in the right ear. If first heard in the left ear it is regarded as a sign of had omen. Both in England and Germany there is a belief among the peasantry that the cuckoo will tell if asked. by the repetition of his cry, how many years the ques- tioner has to live. It is tO this fond and foolish belief that we owe the rhyme
Cuckori, elkerry-tree.l m,.,

THE DOCKS AT WARRINGTON.

It must, however, he noted that it is only a small part of the disused river bed which is tale filled up ; th ttest of the old Mersey channel is not merely not to be filled up, but is to be deepened and extended by the excavating of a considerable portion of the Arplev 'Meadows so as to form the Warrington Docks. In length these docks will extend from a point of the river as it is at present opposite the Warrington Me of et. Janes' Church to a point opposite the cottages which lie mid- way between Wilderspool brewery and Tool Paine's Madge. At the Wildenspool end, the docks will cover a inurh larger surface than at th, Warrington end, so as to allow the necessary space for the turning and massing of vesseLs which, it may be expected, will he continually leaving and entering the canal. From the south-western end of the docks, there will he a means of entering the river thtsough locks. By this arrangement vessels of suitable draught which may have route to Warrington from Manchester on the one hand or Eastham on the other, or indeed front any intermediate place on the canal, can be passed into the river in order to load or unload a cargo at, say, Bank Quay, or, by coming along the new channel, at any place higher up the river whirls is at present navigable.

Other works which will tend to greatly alter the gen- eral features of the view final Arply bridge, will be the construction of a new railway and the deviation of the old lints. The new railway is projected to branch sharply off fneo the Warrington end of Walton Arches and to take a direct route to the docks where, doubtless, it will branch out into many sidings for the convenience of traffic. In its comae it will have to cross the river in its new bed, and this it will do by a bridge. At pre- sent there an-two railways running over Walton Arches, one the Birkenhead, Lancashire, and Cheshire Junction Railway, which carries pAssengers and goods through Daresbury and Prodslom to Chester, and the other the Grand Junction Railway, which runs through Moontand Preston Brook to Crewe, and the farther south, the latter being on the westmost side and running din-ct into Bank Quav high level station. Both of these lines will be deviated, in order that they may be raised Li suffi- cient altitude to on ,s the canal at a high level. The deviation of the Grand Junction Railway will begin near the arches in'' Sluteher's"-lane—the first of the series of arches crossed after kkving Bank Quay Station—and tho line will rise from RUA point 011 !rage embankments at a gradient of one in 135 crossing the river by a new bridge —a sort of second and heightened edition of Walton Arehess—and continuing its upward course will finally reach its highest point on the new viaduct that iota span the ship canal, -a-hen it will gradually descend till it regains its old route. The trains leaving Warrington by the Birkenhead, Lancashire, and Cheshire Junction , Railway will continue as at present to run over Walton Arches, but directly they eross they will turn to the right :on to the deviated line that is to be constructed, and Width, owing to the much shorter length of this devi- ation, will ...arm them by a steeper gradient on to the great ship canal viaduct, after leaving, which they will, as in the ltiter case. descend on to the old line.
